task.title: Apply rules on conditions
task.shortdesc: A conditional rule holds rules that apply only when a condition is true. Use conditions to keep several designs in one stylesheet, to use a feature only where it exists, and to import stylesheets.

info.p: An @media rule holds rules for a medium. CSSMedia makes a PDF, a paged medium, so the type print and the type all are true and the type screen is false. After the type you can test features of the medium in parentheses, joined with and. A comma separates alternatives, not reverses a whole query, and a query with no type has the type all:

A feature can compare with >, <, >= and <=, and you can write a range such as (100pt <= width <= 700pt). The features of the width and the height use the size of an A4 page, whatever size your @page rule sets. The cascade reference lists every media feature with the value that CSSMedia gives it.

An @supports rule applies when CSSMedia accepts the declaration or selector in its condition. A stylesheet can use a new property and keep a fallback for the readers that do not know it. Write a declaration in parentheses, or a selector in selector(), and combine tests with and, or and not. The function at-rule() tests an at-rule:
The test is about the syntax, not about your document: selector(chapter > title) is true even if the document has no chapter.

An @supports-condition rule gives a name to a group of tests, which you use afterwards as (--name) inside @supports. Define the name before you use it. If you define a name twice, the last definition is used:

An @when rule joins media tests and support tests in one condition. Write media() with one media feature, without a type, and supports() with a declaration. Combine them with and, or and not, and group them with parentheses. An @else rule that follows @when, @media, @supports or @container applies only when no branch before it applied. It can have a condition of its own, and without one it is the last fallback:
Only the first branch with a true condition applies. An @else belongs to the conditional rule right before it, and any other rule between them ends the chain.

An @custom-media rule gives a name that starts with two hyphens to a media query, or to true or false. Use the name in parentheses in a media query. A definition can use other names. If you define a name twice, the last definition is used:

An @container rule tests an ancestor of the element instead of the page. It applies to the nearest ancestor that qualifies. A size test, such as (width >= 100pt), needs an ancestor with container-type. A style test, written with style(), compares a custom property of the ancestor, and any element can be the container for it. To choose one ancestor, give it a container-name and write the name before the condition:

An @import rule loads the rules of another stylesheet at that place. Write the URL, or a quoted string, first. After it, you can put the imported rules in a layer with layer(), test the support of a feature with supports() and name the media:

If the condition of an import is false, its rules do not apply. Write all the @import rules at the top of the stylesheet, before any other rule except @charset and layer statements. An @import after another rule is ignored. The rules you write after an import win against the imported rules of the same specificity, because they come later.

An @namespace rule gives a prefix to the namespace of some of your elements, so that selectors can use it, as in a|title. It goes after the imports and before the other rules. Basic selectors and namespaces explains the selectors.
The rules in a @layer block are not conditional, and Decide which rule wins explains them.
